title: Dreaming of the Sky
summary: Long before anyone built a rocket, people stared at the Moon and wished they could go there. They told stories about wings made of wax, ships blown up by whirlwinds and spirits that carried travellers through the dark. But one giant puzzle stood in the way: how do you move where there is nothing to push on?

sections.heading: A Sky Full of Questions
paragraphs: Go outside on a clear night, far from streetlights, and look up. The Moon hangs there, bright and silent. Thousands of stars sparkle. A few brighter dots do not twinkle as much as the rest, and if you watched them for weeks you would see them slowly drift across the background of stars. Every human who has ever lived has seen this same sky, and almost every one of them has wondered what is up there and whether we could ever go and see.

For most of history, the sky was not just scenery. It was a clock, a calendar and a map. Farmers watched for certain stars to know when to plant. Sailors steered by them at night. The Moon's phases, from thin crescent to full and back again in about 29 and a half days, gave many peoples their idea of a month.

Ancient peoples filled the sky with stories. To the Greeks, the Moon was the goddess Selene, driving her silver chariot across the night. In China, a famous legend tells of Chang'e, who swallowed an elixir and floated up to live on the Moon with a jade rabbit for company. These were not science, but they show something important: people had been imagining a journey to the Moon for thousands of years before anyone knew how far away it really was.

Alongside the myths, careful watchers began to measure. In ancient Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq, astronomers wrote down the positions of the Moon and planets on clay tablets for centuries, and learned to predict some eclipses. The Greeks called the drifting lights planetes, which means wanderers, and that is where our word planet comes from. Around 240 BCE, a scholar named Eratosthenes, working in Egypt, used shadows cast by the Sun in two different cities to estimate the size of the whole Earth, and his answer was surprisingly close to the truth.

Other Greek thinkers used eclipses and geometry to work out how far away the Moon was. The astronomer Hipparchus, in the 2nd century BCE, estimated distances of roughly 60 to 80 times the radius of the Earth. That is not far off the real average distance, which is about 60 Earth radii, or about 384,000 kilometres. Think about that: more than two thousand years ago, without telescopes, people had a rough idea of how far you would have to travel to reach the Moon. Knowing how far it is, though, is very different from knowing how to get there.

In fact, the most influential thinker of ancient Greece made the trip seem impossible in principle. Aristotle, in the 4th century BCE, taught that the world below the Moon was made of four elements, earth, water, air and fire, which naturally moved up or down. Above the Moon, he said, everything was made of a perfect fifth substance called aether, moving forever in circles. The heavens were a completely different kind of place, and ordinary things from Earth simply did not belong there. This picture of the universe, later organized in great detail by the astronomer Ptolemy in Alexandria in the 2nd century CE, was taught in schools for well over a thousand years. If the sky is made of a different kind of stuff with different rules, why would anyone even try to fly into it?

sections.heading: Wings of Wax: The Legend of Icarus
paragraphs: Of all the old flying stories, one has been retold more than almost any other. It is a Greek myth, which means it is a legend, not history. Nobody thinks it really happened. But it has inspired poets, painters and inventors for more than two thousand years, and it says something true about the dream of flight.

The story goes like this. Daedalus was the most brilliant craftsman in the world. He was so clever that King Minos of Crete hired him to build the Labyrinth, a maze so tangled that nobody who entered could find the way out. Inside it lived the Minotaur, a monster that was half man and half bull. But when Daedalus fell out of favour, Minos trapped him on the island of Crete together with his young son, Icarus. The king controlled the ships and the harbours. There seemed to be no way off.

Daedalus looked up at the seabirds wheeling above the cliffs and had an idea. If the sea and the land were closed to him, the sky was not. He gathered feathers, small and large, and arranged them in rows like the pipes of a shepherd's flute. He stitched the big feathers together with thread and fixed the small ones with wax. Slowly, he curved them into two great pairs of wings, one for himself and one for his son.

Before they took off, Daedalus gave Icarus a warning. Fly the middle path, he said. Too low, and the spray from the sea will make your feathers heavy. Too high, and the heat of the Sun will melt the wax. Then they leapt into the air. At first all went well. Fishermen and shepherds below stared up, thinking the two flyers must be gods. But Icarus grew bolder and bolder. Thrilled by the feeling of flying, he climbed higher and higher towards the Sun. The wax softened, the feathers slipped away, and Icarus fell into the sea and drowned. The part of the Aegean Sea where he was said to have fallen is still called the Icarian Sea, and a nearby island is named Ikaria.

The best-known telling of this myth comes from the Roman poet Ovid, in his long poem Metamorphoses, finished around the year 8 CE. Centuries later, European artists painted the scene again and again. One famous painting, long thought to be by Pieter Bruegel the Elder, shows a peaceful landscape with a farmer ploughing and a ship sailing by, while in a corner two tiny legs splash into the water. Nobody in the picture even notices.

Of course, the science of the story is backwards. In real life, the higher you climb, the colder the air becomes, not hotter. Mountaineers on Mount Everest face freezing temperatures even though they are closer to the Sun. And human arms are far too weak to flap wings big enough to lift a person. But the myth was never meant to be an engineering manual. It is about dreaming big, about the thrill of leaving the ground, and about the danger of ignoring good advice. Every rocket engineer in this story, from medieval China to modern Florida, has had to balance daring and caution, just as Daedalus tried to teach his son.

sections.heading: A Wooden Pigeon and a Spinning Steam Ball
paragraphs: Did anyone in the ancient world build a machine that moved by itself? Two examples often appear in rocket history books, though neither was a rocket. The first comes from Tarentum, a Greek city in southern Italy, which today is called Taranto. Around 400 BCE, a man named Archytas lived there. He was a serious mathematician, a friend of the philosopher Plato, a respected leader of his city and an army general. According to a story, he also built a wooden model of a dove, or pigeon, that could fly.

Here is the important part: we do not have any description of this pigeon from Archytas's own time. The only ancient account comes from a Roman writer named Aulus Gellius, who lived in the 2nd century CE, around 500 years after Archytas. Gellius said he had read about it in the work of an earlier scholar, Favorinus. According to that report, the dove was balanced with weights and moved by air shut up inside it, and once it landed it could not rise again. Gellius himself seemed to think the tale was rather hard to believe. Many modern books describe the pigeon as hanging on a wire and pushed by escaping steam, but those details are guesses added much later. So the honest answer is that the pigeon is a story known only from writers who lived long after, and we cannot be sure exactly what it was or how it worked, or even whether it existed at all.

The second example is much better documented. Hero (also called Heron) of Alexandria lived in the great city of Alexandria, in Egypt, in the 1st century CE. Historians date him partly because one of his books mentions an eclipse that matches one seen in Alexandria in the year 62 CE. Hero probably taught at the Museum of Alexandria, a famous centre of learning that stood beside the great Library. His books read like lecture notes, full of mathematics, measuring and clever machines.

In one book, called the Pneumatica, which means something like 'about air and breath', Hero described more than a hundred devices worked by air, water and steam. There was a coin-operated machine that gave out a measured squirt of water when you dropped in a coin, a kind of ancient vending machine. There was a pump for spraying water onto fires, an organ played by wind, and singing mechanical birds. And there was a device we now call the aeolipile, after Aeolus, the Greek keeper of the winds.

The aeolipile worked like this. A closed metal pot of water sat over a fire. Two pipes rose up from the lid and held a hollow metal ball between them, so that the ball could turn on the pipes like a wheel on an axle. As the water boiled, steam rushed up through the pipes into the ball. Sticking out from opposite sides of the ball were two small bent tubes, shaped like the letter L and pointing in opposite directions. Steam shot out of these tubes, and as it did, the ball spun round and round, faster and faster.

Why does it spin? Because when the steam is pushed out of a tube one way, the tube, and the ball it is attached to, gets pushed the opposite way. One bent tube pushes the ball one way round, the other tube on the opposite side pushes it the same way round, and so the ball whirls. You may have seen the same thing in a spinning garden sprinkler, whose arms whirl backwards as water squirts out of them. This idea, that throwing something out one way pushes you the other way, is called action and reaction. It is exactly the principle that lifts every rocket. But nobody in Hero's time could explain it with a law of physics. That would have to wait more than 1,600 years.

Was the aeolipile a rocket? No. It was fixed in place, it did not carry its own fuel inside it and it did not go anywhere. It only spun. It was also never put to practical work. As far as we know, it remained a wonderful demonstration, the kind of thing a teacher shows to amaze students. Some historians call it the first recorded steam engine, or the first reaction engine. What it really shows is that nearly 2,000 years ago, a clever engineer had already stumbled on the push that would one day carry people to the Moon, without having any idea how big that idea really was.

sections.heading: Lucian's Ship in a Whirlwind
paragraphs: In the 2nd century CE, about a hundred years after Hero, a witty writer named Lucian was making people laugh all across the Roman Empire. He was born around the year 120 in Samosata, a town on the River Euphrates in what is now southeastern Turkey. His first language was probably not Greek, yet he became one of the sharpest writers in the Greek language, travelling around as a public speaker and poking fun at pompous philosophers, gossipy historians and anyone who took themselves too seriously.

His most famous joke is a book usually called A True Story, or True History. The title itself is part of the joke. In the introduction, Lucian admits that the only true thing in the whole book is that he is telling lies. He was making fun of travel writers of his day, who filled their books with wild reports of monsters and marvels from faraway lands and swore that it was all true. Lucian decided to out-exaggerate them all.

The story begins with Lucian and fifty companions setting sail westward, past the Pillars of Hercules, the rocky gateway where the Mediterranean meets the Atlantic Ocean near today's Strait of Gibraltar. For the ancient Greeks, this was the edge of the known world. A storm drives the ship across the ocean for 79 days. On the 80th day they land on a strange island where they find a river of wine and vines that are women from the waist up.

Then comes the part that makes this book famous in the history of space travel. Soon after they sail on, a mighty whirlwind spins the ship around and lifts it high into the air, far above the sea. The wind keeps pushing the sails, and after about a week of sailing through the sky, the travellers see a great shining island hanging in space. It is the Moon. Looking down, they can see the Earth far below them, with its cities, rivers and seas.

On the Moon, they are captured by soldiers riding enormous three-headed vultures and taken to the king, Endymion. (In Greek myth, Endymion was a handsome shepherd loved by the Moon goddess, so Lucian made him the Moon's ruler.) Endymion is at war with Phaethon, king of the Sun, over who gets to set up a colony on the Morning Star, which is the planet we call Venus. The armies Lucian invents are wonderfully silly: tens of thousands of vulture-riders, giant birds covered in grass with lettuce leaves for wings, soldiers riding huge fleas, and from the Sun's side, warriors on flying ants and others who hurl giant radishes. In the end the Sun's army builds a wall of clouds that blocks the sunlight from the Moon, and the Moon people have to make peace.

A True Story was meant as satire, not science, and you should not read it expecting to learn anything about real space. Lucian imagined that a ship could simply sail upward through air all the way to the Moon, because nobody yet knew that the air gets thinner and thinner and finally ends. But the book is one of the oldest surviving stories about a journey to the Moon, and a group of people from Earth meeting beings who live on other worlds. That is why many writers call it one of the earliest works of science fiction, written about 1,800 years before Star Wars. Lucian may have been joking, but he gave the world a picture that would never go away: people from Earth, looking back at their home planet from the Moon.

sections.heading: Kepler's Dream
paragraphs: Now jump forward about 1,400 years, to central Europe in the early 1600s. The old picture of the universe is crumbling. In 1543, the Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus had published a book arguing that the Earth is not the fixed centre of everything, but a planet that spins and travels around the Sun. If Earth was a planet, then perhaps the planets were worlds, and the Moon was a place, made of rock rather than perfect aether.

One of the people who took this idea most seriously was a German astronomer named Johannes Kepler, who lived from 1571 to 1630. Kepler had poor eyesight from a childhood illness, but he was a mathematical genius. Working with the precise observations of the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe, he discovered that planets travel around the Sun not in perfect circles but in ovals called ellipses, and that they speed up when they are closer to the Sun. In 1610, the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei published what he had seen when he pointed one of the first telescopes at the Moon: mountains, valleys and craters. The Moon was not a perfect crystal ball. It was a world.

Kepler had been thinking about the Moon since he was a student. At the University of Tübingen, in the 1590s, he had worked on a question that Copernicus's ideas raised: what would the sky look like to someone standing on the Moon? Over the years, that question grew into a strange, short book called Somnium, which is Latin for The Dream. Kepler wrote most of it around 1608 to 1609, shared a version in 1611, and kept adding to it for the rest of his life. He did not live to see it printed. It was finally published in 1634 by his son Ludwig, four years after Kepler's death.

The story is wrapped in layers like a set of nesting dolls. A narrator falls asleep while reading and dreams of a book. In that book, a boy named Duracotus grows up in Iceland with his mother, Fiolxhilde, a wise woman who sells herbs and knows secret things. Duracotus goes to Denmark to study astronomy with Tycho Brahe, just as Kepler had worked with Tycho in real life. When he comes home, his mother calls up a daemon, a kind of spirit, from a place called Levania, which is Kepler's name for the Moon.

The daemon explains how travellers can be carried to Levania, and this is where Kepler becomes surprisingly modern. The journey can only happen during a lunar eclipse, when the shadow of the Earth stretches out towards the Moon, because the daemons cannot stand sunlight. The daemon warns that weak or soft people need not apply. The take-off is so violent, it says, that it is like being blasted out by gunpowder, so travellers are given a drug to put them to sleep, and their arms and legs are carefully arranged so that the shock does not tear them apart. There is terrible cold to survive, and the air is so thin that travellers must hold damp sponges to their noses to breathe. Partway through the trip, the travellers' bodies move along towards the Moon by themselves, and near the end the daemons must slow them down so that they do not crash.

Look at the problems Kepler was worrying about: a crushing acceleration at launch, freezing cold, not enough air, and the need to brake before landing. These are real problems that every space agency has had to solve. Kepler used magic to fix some of them, but he was asking the right questions. He even seems to have imagined that the Earth's pull fades with distance until the Moon's pull takes over, decades before Isaac Newton explained gravity.

Most of the Somnium is not about the journey at all. It describes what the sky looks like from Levania. Kepler pointed out that the Moon always keeps the same side towards Earth, so for people on that side, the Earth, which he calls Volva, would hang in the same spot in the sky all the time, never rising or setting, looking far bigger than the Moon looks to us, and going through phases. People on the far side would never see the Earth at all. A day on Levania lasts about two of our weeks, and so does a night, so the ground would bake and then freeze. Kepler imagined enormous snake-like creatures with spongy skins that hide in caves from the scorching heat. The story itself is only about 30 pages long, but Kepler added 223 notes explaining the science, and the notes are several times longer than the story.

The book may also have brought real sorrow into Kepler's life. A handwritten version was passed around years before it was printed. In 1615, Kepler's own mother, Katharina, was accused of witchcraft in her home town in Germany. Kepler suspected that people had read his story about a boy whose mother summons spirits and taken it as being about his family, although historians are not sure the book played any part. Katharina was imprisoned in 1620 and threatened with torture. Kepler travelled to defend her himself, and she was finally released in 1621, dying a few months later. Because of all this, Somnium is often called the first work of science fiction that tried hard to follow real science.

sections.heading: The Wall With No Handholds
paragraphs: By the time Somnium was published, people had a better picture of the Moon than ever before. They knew roughly how far away it was. They had seen its mountains through telescopes. Writers had imagined trips there on wings, on ships lifted by whirlwinds, and in the arms of spirits. But nobody had the faintest idea how a real machine could get there. To see why, think about how everything that moves on Earth actually moves.

When you walk, your feet push backward on the ground, and the ground pushes you forward. A rowing boat moves because its oars push back on the water. A bird flies by pushing air down and back with its wings. Even a sailing ship needs the wind to push on its sails. Every way of travelling that anyone knew in the 1600s needed something outside the traveller to push against: earth, water or air. And a new discovery was about to show that out in space, none of these things exist.

In 1643, an Italian scientist named Evangelista Torricelli filled a long glass tube with mercury, turned it upside down into a bowl of mercury, and watched the silvery liquid sink down to a height of about 76 centimetres, leaving an empty space at the top of the tube. He explained that the column was being held up by the weight of the air pressing down on the bowl. In other words, air has weight, and we live at the bottom of an ocean of it. This was the first barometer.

A few years later, in 1648, the French thinker Blaise Pascal asked his brother-in-law, Florin Périer, to carry one of these tubes up a mountain called the Puy de Dôme in central France. As Périer climbed, the mercury in the tube sank lower and lower, because there was less air above pressing down. The ocean of air got thinner as you went up. And if it got thinner, then somewhere above it must run out completely.

Then a German inventor and mayor named Otto von Guericke built an air pump that could suck most of the air out of a container. In a famous demonstration in the 1650s, he fitted two copper half-spheres together and pumped out the air between them. Teams of horses pulling in opposite directions could not drag the halves apart, because the air pressing on the outside held them together so tightly. The experiment showed that a near-vacuum, a space with almost no air in it, was real and could be made on Earth.

Put all these discoveries together, and you get a giant problem for anyone dreaming of the Moon. The air ends a short distance above our heads. Beyond it lies an enormous emptiness, hundreds of thousands of kilometres of it, with no ground to push against, no water to row through, no air for wings or sails. Lucian's whirlwind and Daedalus's feathers would be useless out there. It was like trying to climb a cliff that has no handholds at all.

What was needed was a machine that carried its own push with it, something that could throw stuff out of its back end and be shoved forward in return, even with nothing around it. Hero's spinning steam ball had hinted at that trick, but steam needs a heavy boiler and a fire, and it is far too weak. Kepler had compared his imaginary launch to a blast of gunpowder, perhaps without realizing how close to the truth he was.

The answer would not come from steam, wax wings or magical spirits. It would come from a strange black powder that hisses, flares and roars, a powder that burns even without air from outside. It had been discovered centuries earlier, on the other side of the world, by alchemists in China who were searching for something completely different: a medicine to help people live forever.

deepDive: Historians of spaceflight love to start with Archytas and Hero, but it is worth being careful about what these devices really were. Archytas's flying dove is a classic example of a 'source problem'. The only ancient report comes from Aulus Gellius's Attic Nights, written in the 2nd century CE, who relays a claim from the scholar Favorinus about a man who had died roughly five centuries earlier. Gellius describes a wooden model balanced by weights and moved by enclosed air, and he treats the tale as hard to believe. Later retellings that mention steam, wires and pulleys are reconstructions, not evidence. Historians therefore treat the dove as an interesting legend rather than an established invention. Hero's aeolipile is on firmer ground because his own text, the Pneumatica, survives. Scholars date Hero to the 1st century CE partly because the astronomer Otto Neugebauer matched an eclipse mentioned in his Dioptra to one seen at Alexandria in 62 CE. The aeolipile is a genuine reaction device: the steam leaving its nozzles carries momentum in one direction, so the sphere gains angular momentum in the other. Engineers sometimes call it the first reaction turbine. But it differs from a rocket in two key ways: its working fluid comes from an external boiler rather than from propellant carried on board, and it produces rotation rather than travel. Its thrust is also tiny. There is a long-running debate about why the ancient world did not turn such devices into useful engines. Common explanations include plentiful slave and animal labour, the lack of strong, precisely machined metal parts, and a scholarly culture that prized theory over practical machinery, though historians warn against any single neat answer. On the literary side, critics argue about which work deserves the title 'first science fiction'. Lucian's True Story (about 160 to 180 CE) features space travel, alien life and interplanetary war, but it is openly satirical and ignores physics. Kepler's Somnium (written about 1608 to 1609, published 1634) is shorter on adventure but uses real astronomy, including Copernican motion, lunar day length and the fixed position of Earth in the lunar sky, which is why writers such as Carl Sagan and Isaac Asimov pointed to it as a founding work of science-based fiction. Both labels depend on how you define the genre.
funFact: Kepler's Somnium is only about 30 pages of story, but he wrote 223 explanatory notes for it, and the notes are several times longer than the tale itself.
